news_drafts.headline: Bridgend accounts clear audit but required material corrections to draft figures
news_drafts.lead: Bridgend Council's auditors gave the council an unqualified audit opinion — a clean bill of health — on its 2024/25 accounts. However, the draft accounts for 2025/26 required material corrections before certification, the Governance and Audit Committee heard. The initial draft omitted transactions and balances from the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee, a material joint venture arrangement, which were added only in September's revised version. Auditors also identified that the council had understated its minimum revenue provision — the amount it must set aside each year to repay past borrowing — by £0.291 million due to incorrect accounting treatment for the purchase of the Rhiw. Member allowances were overstated by £0.061 million. All corrections were made by management before the auditor certified the accounts on 25 September, ahead of the statutory deadline.
news_drafts.paper_title: Covering Report for Governance and Audit Committee Annual Report 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Bridgend faces £19.25m refinancing bill as lender raises rate on decades-old loans
news_drafts.lead: Bridgend Council will repay £19.25 million of bank loans after the lender exercised its right to increase the interest rate from 4.65 per cent to 7.52 per cent, effective 22 July 2026. Rather than accept the higher rate on the LOBO loans—long-term borrowing where lenders may propose rate increases on set dates—the council chose to repay at par and refinance. The repayment comes as the council faces a broader tightening of its financial position. Its underlying need to borrow, the amount it has spent on long-lived assets it has not yet paid for, is forecast to grow from £182.56 million to £200.82 million by March 2028 as capital commitments progress. The council is currently using £69.97 million of its own cash reserves to fund capital spending instead of borrowing, a position the treasury report suggests cannot be sustained indefinitely as reserves deplete.

findings.headline: Bridgend's draft Minimum Revenue Provision was understated by £0.291 million relating to the Rhiw purchase, requiring correction during audit.
findings.detail: An error was identified in the MRP calculation relating to the accounting treatment for purchase of the Rhiw asset. The MRP was understated by £0.291 million and corrected during audit. MRP is the mechanism councils use to ensure they set aside sufficient resources to repay borrowing as it falls due.
findings.matters: MRP controls are fundamental to a council's debt management; an understatement indicates potential pressure on capital financing resources or weaknesses in how capital transactions are accounted for.
findings.quote: Correction identified by the Council Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) understated by £0.291m due to the accounting treatment for the purchase of the Rhiw.

findings.headline: A category of asset valuations was not indexed as required, creating a control weakness that could become materially cumululative over five years.
findings.detail: The auditor identified that indexation had not been applied to a category of Existing Use Value (EUV) assets in the asset register. While the shortfall is not material in 2025-26, the auditor notes it could become cumulatively material over the five-year valuation cycle, indicating a persistent control gap in how assets are managed and valued.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council's control environment reliably produces accurate financial information; undetected control failures that could compound over time pose incremental risk.
findings.figures: Value not specified as immaterial in current year but cumulative risk flagged over five-year cycle
findings.quote: We also identified that indexation had not been applied to a category of EUV assets. The value of these assets is not material to the accounts this year, but indexation could become cumulatively material over the five-year valuation cycle.

findings.headline: Bridgend's initial 2025-26 draft accounts omitted all South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee transactions and balances, which were added only in a revised September draft.
findings.detail: The first draft of the accounts completely failed to include SEW CJC transactions and balances. These were added to a revised draft provided in September based on draft SEW CJC accounts. The auditor found no misstatements once the transactions were included, but this represents a significant gap in the council's financial reporting control process.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the completeness and accuracy of financial reporting controls; missing material transactions entirely from initial draft accounts indicates control weaknesses that could affect future reliability.
findings.figures: SEW CJC transactions are material but figure not specified in this report
findings.quote: The initial 2025-26 draft accounts did not include SEW CJC transactions and balances. These were added to the revised draft provided in September, based on the draft SEW CJC accounts.

findings.headline: Bridgend receives an unqualified audit opinion on its 2025-26 accounts.
findings.detail: The Auditor General for Wales intends to issue an unqualified audit opinion, confirming the accounts give a true and fair view and have been properly prepared in accordance with standards. No uncorrected misstatements above the reporting threshold remain.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that accounts comply with standards and present a reliable picture of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Materiality set at £5.941 million (1% of gross expenditure); reporting threshold £0.297 million
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the accounts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Governance Audit Committee Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Committee questioned whether council is incurring interest on borrowed funds that are not being spent.
findings.detail: During review of Treasury Management and Investment Strategy, the Governance and Audit Committee specifically asked whether the council has borrowed money for capital spending but left it unspent, thereby incurring interest costs without deploying the capital. The committee's note that treasury management was 'working well' suggests they received adequate reassurance, but the specific question raises capital execution efficiency as a topic of review.
findings.matters: Unutilized borrowing increases a council's debt burden and interest costs without delivering the planned capital assets or service improvements; poor capital execution efficiency matters to lenders assessing financial risk.
findings.quote: whether the Council was borrowing money, and therefore paying interest, that was not being used
